Traffic analysis — observing patterns/volumes without altering traffic — is passive. Active = changes something; passive = only observes. Memorize: only one passive option will appear among actives.
d5_192: Trap is A 'computer error' — machines aren't tricked, people are.
Trap is C 'expertise' — attacker may use any skill level.
Trap is D 'technology' — social engineering bypasses tech, exploits humans.
Social engineering succeeds through judgment errors — humans make wrong trust decisions. Root cause is human reasoning failure. Tech can't fix bad judgment.
d5_193: Trap is A 'local network' — too far inside; misses external attacks.
Trap is B 'outside firewall' — would be overwhelmed by Internet noise.
Trap is D 'on the host' — host-based, not network-based.

DMZ placement lets the IDS see traffic that has passed the firewall but is heading to public-facing servers — the right zone for monitoring real threats to the website. Network-based IDS goes where the meaningful traffic is filtered. DMZ = standard placement.
d5_194: Trap is B 'physical resources' — capacity planning, not avail/conf.
Trap is C 'admin training' — operational, not control.
Trap is D 'VM in DR plan' — availability piece but narrower than hardening.

Hardened server configuration is the foundation — VM hosts run multiple guests, so any unhardened surface compromises both availability and confidentiality across all VMs. Hypervisor/host hardening = root of trust. MOST important VM control.
d5_195: Trap is B 'identification' — identity claim, not hash function.
Trap is C 'authorization' — permission decisions, not hashing.
Trap is D 'encryption' — reversible; hashes are one-way.

Hash functions support authentication — message integrity, password verification, digital signatures all use hashes to confirm authenticity. Hashes verify, not encrypt. Most common auditor encounter is in auth flows.
d5_196: Trap is B 'incoming spoofed source' — defends YOU, not against being amplifier.
Trap is C 'IP options set' — old hardening but not amplification-specific.
Trap is D 'incoming to critical hosts' — internal protection, not amplification.

Egress filtering — drop outgoing packets with non-internal source addresses — prevents your network being used as DDoS amplifier (your hosts can't spoof external sources). Egress source-validation = anti-amplification. BCP38.
d5_197: Trap is B 'toxic gases' — that's HVAC/positive pressure, not mantraps.
Trap is C 'starve fire of oxygen' — that's gas suppression.
Trap is D 'rapid movement' — physical effect, but PRIMARY purpose is access control.
Mantrap (two doors with interlock) lets one authorized person enter at a time — directly preventing piggybacking/tailgating. Single-person verified entry. The defining mantrap purpose.
d5_198: Trap is A 'workstation upgrades' — typically not required for SaaS.
Trap is B 'higher long-term cost' — financial concern, not audit-control concern.
Trap is C 'no onsite support' — SaaS by nature is remote-supported.

Undefined incident-handling procedures with the SaaS provider create gaps when breaches occur — who responds, who notifies, what data is preserved. Cloud incidents need contractual clarity. Top SaaS audit concern.
d5_199: Trap is B 'forge with another's private key' — implies stealing the private key, not this scheme's risk.
Trap is C 'public key substitution' — public keys are public; substitution attacks have other defenses.
Trap is D 'private key substitution' — possible but the password compromise is the easier and primary vector.

Storing private key on disk protected only by a password means a compromised password = full impersonation via signature. The password is the single point of failure. MOST significant risk in this scheme.
d5_200: Trap is B 'static electricity' — raised floor doesn't prevent static.
Trap is C 'earthquake shock' — raised floor offers no seismic protection.
Trap is D 'water flood' — raised floor under-area can actually pool water (sometimes good, sometimes bad).
Raised floor protects cabling routed underneath from being walked on, kicked, or damaged. Wires under = wires safe. Primary purpose of computer-room raised flooring.
d5_201: Trap is A 'card swipe' — physical second factor; doesn't enforce data segregation within app.
Trap is C 'user inputs ID/password each transaction' — operationally infeasible.
Trap is D 'expiration on embedded password' — rotates secret but doesn't restrict per-user.

RBAC within the application restricts what each authenticated user can do with the shared DB connection — efficient because permissions live at the app/role layer. Single embedded credential is okay if app enforces user-level RBAC. Practical answer for shared-credential designs.
d5_202: Trap is A 'tools used' — practitioner's choice.
Trap is B 'auditor certifications' — qualifications matter but not most important pre-test.
Trap is D 'IDS enabled' — operational concern; doesn't authorize the test.

Permission from the data owner (in writing) is mandatory — pen-tests without authorization are illegal/unauthorized intrusion. Legal authorization first, technical execution second. ALWAYS the answer for 'most important' pre-test step.
d5_203: Trap is A 'accurate inventory' — byproduct, not greatest benefit.
Trap is C 'reduced unauthorized access' — outcome, but cost/control efficiency is broader.
Trap is D 'regulatory compliance' — secondary benefit.

Classification lets you apply expensive controls only where data warrants them — overall control cost decreases while control effectiveness improves. Risk-proportionate spending. BIG benefit: efficiency.
d5_204: Trap is A 'time stamped independently' — useful but not the integrity proof.
Trap is B 'recorded by multiple systems' — redundancy, not integrity.
Trap is C 'encrypted strongly' — confidentiality, not court-admissibility.
Courts require evidence integrity — proof the log hasn't been altered (hashes, chain of custody). Verified integrity = admissible. Without integrity verification, evidence is challenged.
d5_205: Trap is B 'processes and procedures' — execution layer, downstream of strategy.
Trap is C 'functions and services' — operational layer.
Trap is D 'roles and responsibilities' — organizational, downstream of strategy.
IT governance starts with strategies and policies — they set direction; everything else follows. Quality strategy/policy → quality everything below. Top-of-pyramid first.
d5_206: Trap is B 'SSL' — protects in transit, not against fraudulent legitimate-looking transactions.
Trap is C 'password complexity' — prevents some account takeover, not the fraud itself.
Trap is D 'input validation' — prevents bad data, not fraudulent intent.

Transaction monitoring detects unusual patterns (amount, location, frequency) — the actual control against fraudulent payments. Behavioral/analytical detection. Standard answer for online-payment fraud.
d5_207: Trap is A 'don't leave tokens' — important but token alone is one factor.
Trap is B 'token in laptop bag' — same as above.
Trap is C 'random PIN, no repeats' — content rule, less critical than not exposing it.
Writing down the PIN turns 2FA into 1FA — anyone who steals the token also gets the PIN. PIN must remain in user's head. Defeats two-factor protection if violated.
d5_208: Trap is A 'frequent log review' — operational; doesn't ensure correct deployment.
Trap is C 'training local admin' — important but post-deployment.
Trap is D 'sharing admin duties' — SoD, not deployment success.

Testing and validating rule base before going live is the linchpin — a misconfigured firewall is worse than no firewall (false sense of security). Validate in lab before activating. MOST important deployment factor.
d5_209: Trap is A 'tamper-resistant readers' — physical hardening, secondary.
Trap is B 'badge system backups' — availability of system, not access control.
Trap is D 'log all attempts' — detective.

Promptly deactivating lost/stolen badges prevents unauthorized physical entry — the most important operational control for a badge-entry system. Stale active badges = open door for thieves. Process discipline > technology.
d5_210: Trap is B 'logon spoofing' — defended by strong auth/MFA.
Trap is C 'sniffing/decryption' — VPN encrypts; well-defended.
Trap is D 'gateway compromise' — possible but not 'most prevalent.'

Remote VPN brings home/personal endpoints onto the corporate network — if those endpoints are infected, malware spreads inward via the trusted tunnel. Endpoint hygiene risk = most common VPN issue. The 'sick laptop on the couch' problem.
d5_211: Trap is A 'OTP generator' — different mechanism (token auth).
Trap is B 'provides encryption' — signatures don't encrypt; they sign.
Trap is D 'message confidentiality' — signatures provide authenticity, not secrecy.
Digital signatures validate the source — sender's private key signs, anyone with public key verifies origin. Authenticity, integrity, nonrepudiation — NOT confidentiality. The defining trio.
d5_212: Trap is B 'gain access' — comes after recon.
Trap is C 'deny services' — late stage, often goal.
Trap is D 'evade detection' — concurrent with later phases.
Reconnaissance/information gathering is FIRST — attackers map targets, find vulnerabilities, then exploit. Attack methodology starts with knowing what's there. Step 1 of every attack chain.
d5_213: Trap is B 'AUP signature' — formality; doesn't change behavior.
Trap is C 'monitor social media' — detective, post-exposure.
Trap is D 'block access' — bypassable on personal devices/home networks.
Awareness training changes user behavior on what to share — controls disclosure regardless of platform or device. Tech controls can't follow users home. Education = sustained mitigation.
d5_214: Trap is A 'IPS deployed' — IPS doesn't replace network segregation.
Trap is C 'SSO implemented' — authentication, doesn't address network access risk.
Trap is D 'antivirus' — endpoint, not network access control.

If conference-room ports lead to an isolated/segregated network, no enterprise resources are reachable — the risk is neutralized. Segmentation eliminates the unauthorized-access concern. Network design solution.
d5_215: Trap is A 'report confidentiality' — important but post-test.
Trap is B 'find all weaknesses' — never possible; not the operational concern.
Trap is D 'logging changes' — useful but secondary.

Restoring systems to their original state after the test prevents persistent compromise from leftover testing artifacts (planted files, modified configs). Cleanup = production safety. The test must not become a real breach.
d5_216: Trap is A 'developer training' — possible cause but symptom-level.
Trap is B 'admin disabled controls' — investigation later.
Trap is D 'requirements no longer valid' — different scenario.

Verify whether security requirements were specified in the project plan FIRST — root-cause check. Missing controls likely trace to missing requirements. Always trace to requirements before assigning blame.
d5_217: Trap is A 'personal firewall' — host-level last resort, after other layers.
Trap is D 'VLAN config' — network segmentation, less directly defensive than IDS detection of intrusion.
Once the firewall is breached, the IDS is the next defense layer — detecting intrusion that got past the perimeter. Defense in depth: firewall → IDS → host controls. Standard layering question.
d5_218: Trap is A 'user/password policies' — protect login, not URL/DNS routing.
Trap is B 'awareness' — helps but pharming bypasses user-visible cues.
Trap is C 'IDS/IPS' — perimeter defense, doesn't fix DNS poisoning.

Pharming redirects users via poisoned DNS (or hosts file) to fake banking sites — DNS server hardening (DNSSEC, secure config) is the direct defense. Attack the attack vector. DNS = the pharming choke point.
d5_219: Trap is A 'better algorithm' — strengthens crypto, not the protocol weakness.
Trap is C 'frequent password changes' — challenge-response uses session secrets, not user passwords.
Trap is D 'longer auth strings' — incremental.

Session hijacking (replay/intercept of the response) is the main weakness — adding anti-hijacking measures (timestamps, sequence numbers, mutual auth) most directly secures challenge-response. Address the protocol's actual attack surface. Tactical fit.
d5_220: Trap is B 'gray box' — partial knowledge; doesn't guarantee full path coverage.
Trap is C 'black box' — no internals; can't reach all paths.
Trap is D 'dynamic' — runtime testing; doesn't ensure path coverage.
White-box testing uses source code knowledge to design tests covering every code path including error handlers. Path coverage = white-box specialty. Memorize: 'every code path' = white box.
d5_221: Trap is A 'device + origin auth' — proves who, not what wasn't altered.
Trap is B 'wireless IDS/IPS' — detection/prevention of attacks, not integrity proof.
Trap is D 'packet headers/trailers' — addressing/framing, not integrity check.
Cryptographic hashes detect any alteration in transit — recipient recomputes hash and compares. Hash mismatch = altered. Integrity = hashes (HMAC, etc.). Direct definitional answer.
d5_222: Trap is A 'WEP' — broken cipher; obsolete.
Trap is B 'MAC filtering' — easily spoofed; weak.
Trap is C 'disable SSID broadcast' — security through obscurity.
WPA2 (with strong key) is the modern minimum-acceptable wireless security — strong encryption and authentication. WEP/MAC/SSID-hiding all defeated. WPA2 (or WPA3) = the answer.
d5_223: Trap is A 'implicit deny last' — best practice; correct configuration.
Trap is C 'allow/deny rules' — that's the firewall's job.
Trap is D 'VPN endpoint' — common, valid use.

Default OS settings = unhardened = exploitable services, default credentials, open ports underneath the firewall application. Software firewall is only as strong as the OS hosting it. Hardening must precede deployment.
d5_224: Trap is A 'too many alerts' — IDS problem, not IPS-blocking risk.
Trap is B 'performance loss' — operational, not the GREATEST risk.
Trap is D 'specialized expertise' — staffing concern.

IPS blocks inline — false positives cause legitimate critical traffic to be dropped, taking down systems/services. Availability impact from false positives is the IPS-specific top risk. The price of inline prevention.
d5_225: Trap is A 'no RA for compromise reports' — operational gap but secondary.
Trap is C 'cert contains public key' — that's correct/by design.
Trap is D 'report compromises to CA' — correct procedure.

Stale CRL means revoked (compromised) certificates are still trusted by relying parties — direct authentication failure. Fresh CRL is essential to revocation working. MOST significant verification risk.
d5_226: Trap is A 'sender only' — sender computes to sign, but verification needs receiver to recompute.
Trap is B 'receiver only' — sender must compute first to sign.
Trap is D 'CA' — CA issues certs, doesn't compute message digests.

Sender computes digest to sign with private key; receiver recomputes digest and compares to decrypted signature. Both ends compute the digest — that's how integrity is verified. Symmetric computation.
d5_227: Trap is A 'shared secret password' — symmetric secret; doesn't prove origin uniquely.
Trap is B 'encrypt with receiver's public key' — confidentiality, not origin.
Trap is C 'PDF format' — packaging, not authentication.
Digital signature with sender's private key — only sender holds that key, so verification with sender's public key proves origin. Private-key signing = origin authentication. Definitional answer.
d5_228: Trap is A 'no login screen' — guest networks may be open by design.
Trap is C 'guests not isolated from each other' — concern but lateral guest-to-guest is less than guest-to-production.
Trap is D 'single-factor auth' — guest networks rarely need MFA.

Not segregating guest from production network is the GREATEST concern — visitors can reach internal corporate resources directly. Whole point of guest network is segregation. Failure of fundamental design.
d5_229: Trap is A 'SHA-256' — hash, not encryption (passwords stored as hashes don't 'encrypt').
Trap is C 'SSH' — channel/protocol, not at-rest encryption.
Trap is D '3DES' — legacy; weaker and slower than AES.
AES is the current standard for symmetric encryption — strongest among the listed encryption options for storing/encrypting database passwords. AES > 3DES; SHA is hashing. Modern symmetric standard.
d5_230: Trap is B 'data encrypted ready to store' — operational, not C&A purpose.
Trap is C 'tested on different platforms' — portability, not security.
Trap is D 'waterfall phases' — methodology, not C&A.

Certification = technical security evaluation (does it meet security requirements?); accreditation = management acceptance to operate. C&A confirms security compliance via technical evaluation. Memorize: certification → technical, accreditation → management decision.
d5_231: Trap is A 'eavesdropping' — listening to plaintext; encrypted data foils this.
Trap is B 'spoofing' — identity attack, not info gathering.
Trap is D 'masquerading' — impersonation, not pattern analysis.
Traffic analysis examines metadata (volumes, timing, parties) to infer info even when content is encrypted. Encryption hides what; it doesn't hide that. Direct attack on encrypted networks.
d5_232: Trap is A 'integrity' — important but interface auth is the trust foundation.
Trap is B 'confidentiality' — secondary depending on data.
Trap is D 'availability' — operational, not interface-trust.

Across system interfaces, knowing the data really came from the claimed system (data authentication) is critical — wrong source = corrupted commerce. Authentication of inter-system messages is the exchange's foundation. Most critical for B2B/system-to-system.
d5_233: Trap is A 'highest EER' — highest = WORST.
Trap is C 'FRR = FAR' — that IS the EER definition; not by itself the 'most effective' marker.
Trap is D 'FRR = FER' — distractor; mixes unrelated metrics.
Lowest EER = lowest crossover error rate = MOST effective biometric system overall. EER is the single comparison metric; lower wins. Memorize: low EER = good system.
d5_234: Trap is B 'unique ID + password' — both 'know' factors; single factor.
Trap is C 'iris + fingerprint' — both 'are' factors; single factor.
Trap is D 'magstrip + proximity card' — both 'have' factors; single factor.
Smart card (have) + PIN (know) = two DIFFERENT factor types = true 2FA. Two factors must be from DIFFERENT categories (know/have/are). Classic 2FA pattern.
d5_235: Trap is B 'cards not labeled with org name' — labeling lost cards aids adversaries finding building.
Trap is C 'separate departments cause lead time' — operational nuisance.
Trap is D '3-week replacement' — availability concern, not access control.

Generic cards + sign-in without ID proof means anyone claiming to be cleaning staff can enter — accountability and authentication both fail. Identity verification at entry is the basic control. MOST concerning physical-access weakness.
d5_236: Trap is A 'overwritten not reformatted' — overwriting at sector level IS sanitization; format adds nothing.
Trap is C 'hole punch through platters' — physical destruction; effective.
Trap is D 'escorted shredding' — controlled physical destruction.

Logical delete + format does NOT erase data — files are still recoverable via forensic tools. Greatest concern because hard disks leave the org with recoverable sensitive data. Format ≠ wipe. Classic disposal misconception.
d5_237: Trap is A 'reject because policy' — rigid; fails business need.
Trap is B 'approve exception' — bypasses risk analysis.
Trap is D 'revise OS baseline' — premature; baseline shouldn't change for one app.
Risk-based exceptions: assess risk of the deviation, identify compensating controls, then decide. Risk analysis precedes decision. Standard exception-management pattern.
d5_238: Trap is A 'stateful firewall' — connection-level rules; doesn't classify content.
Trap is C 'cache server' — performance, not policy.
Trap is D 'proxy' — channel for traffic; only filters when paired with content rules.
Web content filters classify URLs/categories and block forbidden sites — purpose-built for the policy described. The right tool for the job. Direct match between technology and policy.
d5_239: Trap is B 'IT contingency' — broader IT recovery, not attack-specific.
Trap is D 'continuity of operations' — government/large-org continuity.
Incident Response Plan specifically addresses unauthorized activity — detect, contain, eradicate, recover. Attack-specific lifecycle. Memorize: IRP = attacks; BCP/DRP = business/IT-wide outages.
d5_240: Trap is A 'confidentiality' — encryption, not hashing.
Trap is B 'nonrepudiation' — digital signature, not hash alone.
Trap is C 'authenticity' — needs sender verification, not just hash.
Recomputing the hash on receipt and comparing proves data wasn't altered in transit — integrity. Hash = integrity. Memorize the one-line mapping.
d5_241: Trap is B 'forward the alert' — minor information-leak risk.
Trap is C 'individual solutions' — uncoordinated remediation, secondary concern.
Trap is D 'fail to understand' — miscommunication, not actionable harm.

Detailed threat descriptions can be reverse-engineered into attack playbooks by malicious insiders or recipients — the GREATEST concern. CSIRT info should be sanitized for general distribution. Need-to-know for sensitive details.
d5_242: Trap is B 'vulnerabilities patched' — patch management metric, not IR effectiveness.
Trap is C 'apps protected' — coverage, not response effectiveness.
Trap is D 'pen tests successful' — testing metric.
Financial impact per incident is the outcome metric — effective response = lower per-incident cost. Faster, better response → less damage. Outcome-based KPI for IR.
d5_243: Trap is A 'prior audit reports' — input but doesn't define current scope.
Trap is B 'business strategy' — context, not driver.
Trap is D 'audit deliverables' — outputs, not setting objectives.
Risk assessment reports drive what to audit and how deeply — risk-based auditing's foundation. Risk → priority → scope/objectives. Most directly establishes audit objectives and coverage.
d5_244: Trap is A 'diskless workstations' — preventive infrastructure, not detection.
Trap is C 'antivirus' — detects malware, not licensed-vs-unlicensed software.
Trap is D 'instant dismissal policy' — policy, not detection.

Periodic hard-drive checks (software inventory scans) reveal what's actually installed — direct identification of illegal software. Verify the concern empirically. Detective control fits the validation question.
d5_245: Trap is A 'symmetric encryption' — confidentiality only; no nonrepudiation.
Trap is B 'digital signatures' — integrity + nonrepudiation; not confidentiality.
Trap is C 'message digest' — integrity only.

Digital certificates within a PKI bundle public-key encryption (confidentiality), signing (integrity), and identity binding (nonrepudiation). Full PKI = all three properties. Comprehensive secure-email solution.
d5_246: Trap is A 'no lockout after 5' — bad but reusable shared admin creds is worse.
Trap is B 'password reuse in window' — policy gap, secondary.
Trap is D 'no automated expiration' — operational gap, secondary.

Shared admin credentials destroy accountability for the highest-privilege accounts — can't tell who did what at root. Privileged shared accounts = top auth concern. Worst combo: high power + no attribution.
d5_247: Trap is A 'no significant risk' — wrong; SoD violation present.
Trap is B 'soft zoning risk' — admin says hard zoning; not the issue.
Trap is C 'disabling unused ports' — that's good practice.
SAN admin implemented, tested, documented, AND is sole admin — total lack of SoD and oversight. One person controls everything = greatest risk. Concentration of duty without independent review.
d5_248: Trap is A 'operators read sensitive data' — concern, but printing copies is broader breach.
Trap is B 'data amended' — controls usually exist on spool integrity.
Trap is D 'output lost in failure' — availability, lower than confidentiality.
Unauthorized print copies = uncontrolled hardcopy distribution of sensitive reports outside organization. Once printed, no audit trail or recall. MOST serious spool exposure.
d5_249: Trap is B 'maximize performance' — productivity, secondary.
Trap is C 'enterprise image' — reputational, secondary.
Trap is D 'prevent legal issues' — compliance side-benefit.
Web/email filters block viruses, malicious sites, and inappropriate content — PRIMARY security/operational purpose. Protection > productivity > reputation. The technical security purpose dominates.
d5_250: Trap is A 'screening router' — network-layer filtering only.
Trap is B 'packet filter' — header-level rules; coarse.
Trap is D 'circuit gateway' — session-level control; not application-aware.
Application gateway / proxy understands application protocols (HTTP, FTP, SMTP) — can enforce fine-grained content rules. Layer-7 = highest granularity. Memorize: application gateway = most control.
d5_251: Trap is A 'differential' — scoping/diff report, not a risk type.
Trap is B 'false-positive' — wastes time, not the most serious.
Trap is D 'less detail' — usability issue.
False negatives miss real vulnerabilities — provide false confidence in security posture. Undetected weakness = exploited weakness. Always more dangerous than false positive.
d5_252: Trap is A 'patch immediately' — depends on vendor; gap during the wait.
Trap is B 'block at perimeter' — internal hosts can still infect each other.
Trap is C 'block between segments' — partial; same-segment spread continues.
Stopping the vulnerable services entirely removes the worm's attack surface — most reliable until patches are applied. No service = nothing to exploit. Compensating control during patch lag.
d5_253: Trap is A 'sender's private then sender's public' — that's signing, not confidentiality.
Trap is B 'recipient's private encrypt' — private keys never encrypt outgoing for confidentiality.
Trap is C 'sender's private encrypt' — that's signing.
Confidentiality = encrypt with recipient's PUBLIC key, decrypt with recipient's PRIVATE key. Only the recipient (private-key holder) can read it. Memorize: public-key encrypt = confidentiality.
d5_254: Trap is B 'application gateway' — single device, single layer.
Trap is C 'packet filter router' — basic, not best.
Trap is D 'circuit-level gateway' — single layer.
Screened subnet (DMZ with two firewalls) provides layered defense — outside firewall, DMZ, inside firewall. Multiple barriers = best Internet protection. Defense-in-depth architecture.
d5_255: Trap is A 'inherently linear' — neural networks are nonlinear.
Trap is B 'small training data' — actually need LARGE training sets.
Trap is D 'assumes curve shape' — opposite; no shape assumptions.
Neural networks excel where many input variables interact in complex nonlinear ways — fraud detection's hallmark. Multi-variable pattern recognition. Right fit for fraud's complexity.
d5_256: Trap is C 'AES' — strong but more compute/key-size for equivalent security.
Trap is D 'Blowfish' — less efficient on mobile than ECC.
Elliptic Curve Cryptography provides equivalent security with shorter keys — ideal for mobile devices' limited compute/battery. Strong + efficient = mobile fit. Standard mobile-crypto answer.
d5_257: Trap is A 'digest with sender's private' — that's signing.
Trap is B 'session with sender's public' — wrong key direction.
Trap is C 'message with receiver's private' — private key never encrypts inbound.

Encrypt the session key with the receiver's PUBLIC key — only the receiver can decrypt to obtain the session key, then use it for symmetric encryption of bulk data. Hybrid encryption pattern. Same logic as d5_253.
d5_258: Trap is B 'shred bins in copy rooms' — partial coverage; misses other docs.
Trap is C 'media disposal policy' — paper, not the policy domain.
Trap is D 'shredders in offices' — partial; behavior must support use.
Awareness training teaches employees what to shred and why — drives behavior change at the root. Without awareness, shredders go unused. Awareness = behavior; equipment = capability. Behavior wins.
d5_259: Trap is A 'SSL for admin' — secure remote admin is good practice.
Trap is B 'updated policies' — good practice.
Trap is C 'inbound block by default' — good practice (deny-by-default).
Firewall installed on default-OS configuration leaves the underlying OS exploitable — attacker bypasses firewall by attacking the host. Hardened OS is prerequisite. Same theme as d5_223.
d5_260: Trap is B 'SSID with org name' — broadcasting org name aids attackers.
Trap is D 'SNMP' — monitoring; not security.

Physically securing access points prevents tampering, factory resets, and unauthorized cable taps — physical compromise undermines all logical controls. Physical security is foundational. Choose the only intact-defense option.
d5_261: Trap is B 'admins skipping change control on patches' — bad practice but not direct fraud.
Trap is C 'ops changing batch schedules' — operational issue.
Trap is D 'DBA changing structures' — DBA's job (with controls).
Application programmers changing PRODUCTION DATA = SoD violation enabling fraud (alter records, hide tracks). Dev access to prod data = textbook fraud risk. Highest fraud-likelihood combo.
d5_262: Trap is A 'forget to encrypt' — process risk, secondary to credential exposure.
Trap is B 'creds via email' — concern but split across separate emails reduces single-point compromise.
Trap is D 'shared FTP user ID' — accountability gap.

Consulting firm personnel can access the FTP repository with sensitive financial data — third-party insider risk is the GREATEST concern. Outsider becomes insider via support role. Provider personnel = trust risk.
d5_263: Trap is A 'firewall exists' — firewall doesn't validate code legitimacy.
Trap is B 'secure web connection' — protects transit, not source authenticity.
Trap is D 'host site is enterprise' — origin assumption, not signed-source verification.

Active code is reasonable only when its source is authenticated (signed code from trusted publisher). Trust based on code-signing, not transport or location. Authenticity of executable origin = the gating control.
d5_264: Trap is A 'parity' — single-bit error detection only; misses bursts.
Trap is B 'echo check' — round-trip; basic.
Trap is C 'block sum' — better than parity, weaker than CRC for bursts.
Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) detects burst errors via polynomial division — designed exactly for this. Standard burst-error detector in network frames. Memorize: CRC = burst errors.
d5_265: Trap is A 'copper wire' — easy to tap inductively.
Trap is B 'shielded twisted pair' — shielding helps but still tappable.
Fiber-optic cables transmit light — can't be passively tapped without breaking the cable (which is detectable). Physical-tap resistant. BEST wired-media security choice.
d5_266: Trap is B 'interview admin' — verbal claim, not evidence.
Trap is C 'review procedures' — what should happen, not what does.
Trap is D 'review device logs' — operational events, not configuration state.
Examining the actual parameter settings is direct evidence of compliance vs. policy. Inspect the real config. Verify ≠ trust statements or procedures. Audit inspects the artifact.
d5_267: Trap is A 'shared equipment' — by VoIP design; not the greatest concern.
Trap is C 'voice not encrypted on LAN' — concern but secondary.
Trap is D 'same support team' — operational.

Without UPS on Ethernet switches, a power blip kills both data AND voice — call center loses all phone capability. VoIP makes power = phones. Availability of voice now depends on data infrastructure power.
d5_268: Trap is B 'full backup daily' — recovery, not continuity.
Trap is C 'repair contract' — reactive, not preventive.
Trap is D 'duplicate at each server' — host-level, not WAN.
Built-in alternative routing reroutes traffic around link failures automatically — sustains WAN connectivity during outages. Path redundancy = continuity. WAN-level continuity answer.
d5_269: Trap is A 'strict SLA' — that's a positive.
Trap is B 'no unlimited audit right' — common; manageable with sample/pooled audits.
Trap is C 'no DR plan in SLA' — concern but data-residency tops it for HR data.

HR/PII data spread across multiple cities/countries triggers cross-border data-protection law conflicts (GDPR, sovereignty, transfer restrictions). Jurisdictional risk for personal data. GREATEST cloud-PII concern.
d5_270: Trap is A 'availability' — lock-in doesn't directly affect uptime.
Trap is D 'scalability' — growth capacity, separate from lock-in.
Lock-in clauses prevent moving workloads/data to another provider — removing them protects portability. Portability = freedom to migrate. Direct lock-in inverse.
d5_271: Trap is A 'inheritance' — reuse of class properties, not security.
Trap is D 'polymorphism' — multiple forms, not security.
Encapsulation hides internal data behind defined interfaces — directly enhances security by enforcing access controls at the object boundary. Hide data = protect data. OO security primitive.
d5_272: Trap is B 'capacity adequate' — 96% routinely is dangerous; bursts will saturate.
Trap is C 'replace immediately' — premature without traffic-pattern analysis.
Trap is D 'tell users to reduce' — user-blame, not engineering response.
96% peak suggests imminent saturation under any spike — analyze patterns to determine if saturation/loss occurs and when. Investigate before deciding action. Audit-style 'gather data first' response.
d5_273: Trap is A 'redundant pathways' — network continuity, not server failure.
Trap is C 'dial backup lines' — comm backup, not server.
Trap is D 'standby power' — power continuity, not server failure.
Server clustering shares load and fails-over automatically when a node fails — direct mitigation for server failure impact. Cluster member down = others carry load. Server-level continuity answer.
d5_274: Trap is A 'transaction omission/duplication' — handled by app-level controls.
Trap is B 'data transition' — irrelevant to time sync.
Trap is C 'email timestamps' — minor benefit.

Synchronized clocks let log events from different systems be correlated chronologically — the bedrock of incident investigation/forensics. Without sync, can't reconstruct timeline. MAIN reason for time sync (NTP).
d5_275: Trap is A 'good practices for type' — preceded by importance.
Trap is B 'missing components' — assessment, after importance.
Trap is D 'subcomponents used appropriately' — detailed review, after importance.

Identifying importance/criticality of devices in the topology FIRST establishes what to focus on — risk-based scoping. Critical device → deeper review. Scope by criticality before drilling into config.
d5_276: Trap is A 'admin-only access' — confidentiality, not integrity.
Trap is B 'log at OS layer' — same system as firewall; integrity at risk if firewall is compromised.
Trap is C 'dual log to separate storage' — duplication, but local.

Sending logs to a dedicated remote (third-party) log server immediately means compromised firewall can't tamper with already-shipped logs. Off-system = tamper-evident. Standard log-integrity pattern (SIEM).
d5_277: Trap is A 'no on-site assessment' — concern, manageable via certifications/reports.
Trap is C 'different jurisdictions' — addressable contractually.
Trap is D 'older browser' — client-side issue, not provider gap.
SLA silence on breach responsibility means, at the worst moment, no one is contractually responsible — major liability gap. Breach response is THE key cloud term. Definitional cloud-audit concern.
d5_278: Trap is B 'version usage' — manual tracking, not automated.
Trap is C 'parity' — bit-level integrity, not file identity.
Trap is D 'file security' — access control, not file-correctness.
File header records contain metadata identifying the file (date, version, source) — system reads header automatically to confirm correct file. Self-identifying input. Standard automated check.
d5_279: Trap is A 'input accuracy' — data validation, not transmission.
Trap is B 'downloaded program integrity' — hash checks for that.
Trap is C 'encryption adequacy' — cryptographic strength, not CRC.
CRC validates that transmitted data arrived without corruption — transmission validity. Memorize: CRC = transmission validity / burst-error detection.
d5_280: Trap is B 'increase bandwidth' — premature; root cause unknown.
Trap is C 'baseline + QoS' — useful but after root cause known.
Trap is D 'VLAN segment' — design change, premature.

Use a protocol analyzer + review LAN error logs FIRST to diagnose root cause — random slowness can be many things (errors, broadcast storms, malware). Diagnose before remediating. First-principle troubleshooting.
d5_281: Trap is A 'automated logging' — detective, useful but doesn't verify approval.
Trap is B 'add staff' — not feasible for small enterprise.
Trap is D 'access controls preventing modifications' — would block the legitimate need.

Procedures verifying only APPROVED changes go to production = compensating control for missing SoD in small orgs. Independent review/approval substitutes for separation. Standard small-enterprise SoD compensation.
d5_282: Trap is A 'inventory and categorize' — early step, but ranking drives the plan.
Trap is C 'identify critical systems' — input.

Ranking systems by risk and deciding priority/resources/schedule/frequency IS the audit plan — translates risk into actionable plan. Plan is the output of risk-based approach. MOST important step in PLAN development.
d5_283: Trap is A 'links to ERM' — benefit but not the main one.
Trap is C 'identify residual risk' — partial scope.
Risk-based audit's MAIN benefit is providing the board with assurance that risk management is effectively keeping risk within appetite. Ultimate assurance to governance. Top-of-house benefit.
d5_284: Trap is B 'violated laws' — disclosure to authorities required only if known unlawful and based on evidence.
Trap is C 'not violated — committed to disclose' — incomplete duty; suspected fraud must be reported, not deferred.
Trap is D 'not violated — lack of evidence' — auditor still must report SUSPECTED fraud.

Auditing standards require auditors to report SUSPECTED fraud to appropriate authorities/management, not to defer to QA review. Suspicion + evidence-gathering must escalate. Standard duty-to-report rule.
